title: Panel: Agentic AI in Finance & Legal

segments.text: MATT CARBONARA: Now, we have 25 or so minutes
to chat about the use of agents in legal and finance.
So maybe just to start, maybe your voice is tired,
so we'll start with Nikhil.
When you think about agents and applying them
to these higher risk areas, like finance and transactions
or legal, what are the difference
in requirements between those agents and agents for other use
cases?
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: Yeah.
Thank you.
Look, all finance and legal organizations
that I know of today are already using agents in some fashion,
because they're using coding agents.
And coding agents have this amazing property
around verifiability and testability.
You can go in and read the code.
You can decide if it is too verbose, not verbose enough,
has design docs, doesn't have design docs,
all of that stuff associated with it.
And you can run a test suite against it
and make sure that the agent is doing
what it's supposed to be doing.
With finance and legal, I think you can do the same things,
but the cost of failure is much higher.
So I think if we are doing SOX compliance or we are getting
earnings ready, and we have an agent that his job is to get
earnings ready, and I know this because we have earnings next
week, we cannot take a mistake.
I think the scrutiny of that agent is going to be tremendous.
And so I think the auditability of the decision-making
that the agent is doing, the kind of data sources
that the agent has access to, the verifiability of the output,
all move up to a really, really, really high bar.
And yeah, I mean, I think we're doing this right now.
These are one of the last flows to get
automated, because so much of the company's existence
depends on its ability to get finances right,
to make sure that its legal surface
area is the right, appropriate legal surface area.
And this is also true in other functions in companies
like Circle, like compliance, we don't
want to get hauled in by regulators
just because our agent made a mistake.
They're going to hold us responsible, not the agent.
MATT CARBONARA: Makes sense.
Thank you.
FARAZ SHAFIQ: Can I jump on?
MATT CARBONARA: Please.
Yeah.
Please.
FARAZ SHAFIQ: One very important point.
So I fully agree with Nikhil.
There's a concept called verifiers law.
So what that concept tells you is that tasks that
are easy to verify, those are going
to be ripe for agentic processes.
So imagine Sudoku.
So Sudoku, the puzzle, it's hard to do but very easy to verify.
So anything that's easy to verify-- and coding
is one of those things, where you
do have QA and things like that, where
you can test it very quickly.
But then things that are hard to verify will be harder to solve
and will have a longer lead time.
Self-driving, same thing.
It's very hard to fully verify that was
the car or the vehicle doing the right thing at the right time.
Same thing in banking.
When we have, for example, someone come in and submit
for a credit card application or a loan application, some cases,
we don't have a lot of data.
So if we make an incorrect decision based
on the information we have, and let's just say,
the person defaults, it may be five years from when
they default. So the decision to give them credit was today,
the verification is five years down the road,
becomes very hard.
And so we do look at the verification part of it
as, hey, which are the tasks that are really ripe for agents
that will surpass human, call it probability of being correct
all the time?
And those would be the ones that we would always start with.
MATT CARBONARA: Makes sense.
And I assume, that applies for both in-house agents
that you would build as well as third party
agents that you would buy.
Or do you treat those any differently,
whether they're internally sourced or externally sourced?
FARAZ SHAFIQ: I think there's going to be hybrid.
The big thing is that, as I mentioned in my talk
as well, the models, the intelligence is largely
going to be the same.
So we understand that.
But then there's things that, for example, Wells Fargo
will have in its IP, in its data that others will not.
And so there will be an advantage of having, call it
homegrown agents that are doing certain things.
At the same time, the models and both the,
call it off-the-shelf agents are becoming so powerful right out
of the box, that it just doesn't make sense to not use them.
I think the big thing will be, the economics of them
is, as soon as they start coming down,
they're going to be more pervasive.
Another big thing that we're looking at
is, how would the agents connect to each other?
Because, again, I gave the example
of a home mortgage process.
It is a very large, very complex, roughly,
1,100-step process that we have in the bank.
It will not be one agent.
It's not going to be a collection of agents
that's just homegrown.
It'll be a combination of many things.
And it's not going to be that this agent does a job really
well, but the other one doesn't, because they
need to talk and connect to each other,
especially when the systems are long running.
You give a prompt, you get a response back,
that's easy, that you'll be right.
But when you want something done over multiple hours, or days,
or weeks, the context, that's where it starts
getting a little bit shady.
MATT CARBONARA: Yeah.
And is there an approach?
Or do you know?
Or maybe this is an opportunity for entrepreneurs,
for the things that take longer, that are harder to verify,
any techniques people are using?
Or is that an opportunity for like, hey, we made a decision
today, but it had an impact five years later,
but you don't have that data or you haven't
started to collect that data?
FARAZ SHAFIQ: I would say, if there's entrepreneurs
in the room, agentic harness, for example,
the concept sounds so simple.
It's a harness that holds everything together and sits
on top of the agent.
But it is incredibly hard to do, again, especially
for long running processes.
So that's something that we're actively looking at.
And the stuff that I'm talking about
are industry-specific problems.
These are not just Wells Fargo problems,
these are industry-specific problems.
So anyone who's focused on, for example,
making the agent to agent work, there's
a lot of protocols out there.
A to is A great one.
A lot of organizations also are building
on top of standard SDKs.
So that typically, is not the issue.
The issue is optimizing which data to grab for what task.
How would, for example, a ServiceNow agent collaborate
with Salesforce agent, collaborate
with the home grown agent, share the right context
and the right information?
Very difficult to do so.
That is a big, big opportunity.
MATT CARBONARA: Awesome.
And Nikhil, when you think about agents
in your past lines of work or at Circle,
how do you measure reliability?
What are the metrics that you look at the KPIs?
And how do you determine when an agent is good enough
to put into production?
Or is that variable based on the use case?
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: I mean, most definitely, varies by use case.
I think I attended this talk today morning,
it talked about evals and how evals are really hard.
And the speaker made this point that across organizations,
each organization is idiosyncratic on evals.
I would say, within organizations,
each team is idiosyncratic about evals.
And so what to measure, how to measure, what is good,
needs to be defined process by process by process.
And so we are just standing up the frameworks
for scalable evals.
And then evals break for all kinds of reasons.
There can be model drift.
There can be data issues.
There can be all manners of things
that'll break how an agent is performing.
And so I would say, for the places that we have implemented,
we have tried to lock down both the model, the harness,
and the amount of variables that are going into it,
outside of the input that is coming in.
We do evals.
We also do some of this, where we do
the agent sits with the human.
I think some people call it shadowing.
And we observe how the human is going to do it.
And we observe what the agent is going to do it.
And I guess that's another kind of eval,
if you want to call it that, but we do it differently.
So you simultaneously, on the job,
like compliance analyst gets an inbound.
They're making a decision.
They're looking at what the agent is doing.
And then we evaluate that.
And we run it in a reinforcement learning loop.
So that's how we're measuring it.
The other KPIs we are trying to figure out
is, how much of token spend equates
to what kind of automation we can achieve?
And I think our metrics are really fussy there.
I think right now, we're not focused
on trying to save money on the tokens.
We're like letting people use the tokens and saying,
OK, well, how much productivity can you achieve?
And that productivity often shows up
as either poor human, more output.
That's typically how we're measuring things.
Or in some places, it shows up as revenue.
Those places are small still.
Or there's some other cost-saving that is obvious.
Or we're able to substitute that labor that
was doing x to do y, that's another way KPI show up.
So it's all of the above.
But yeah, there's no rule of thumb in saying like, well, this
is how you do KPIs or eval.
MATT CARBONARA: Makes sense.
Makes sense.
Faraz, you've talked about the importance of the harness layer,
but when you think about building new agents,
you can look at the model, you can pick the model,
you can optimize the model, you can
build the harness, you can look at the workflow,
integrate with the workflow in different ways,
provide different context, memory.
I guess, those are all part of the harness.
But when you think about that engineering effort,
how do you weight the effort against those different elements
when you're trying to build an agent?
FARAZ SHAFIQ: Yeah, I know.
That's where I spent a lot of time,
because think of a traditional product development lifecycle.
You would have an idea.
That idea, again, would go back and forth
into a lot of iterations, typically,
on a Word doc or PowerPoint.
And then you would engage engineering to build a Figma,
build some type of prototype.
And then it would get into that development lifecycle, where,
again, architectural patterns would come in.
You'd look at vulnerabilities, and risk assessment,
and things like that.
So again, the traditional development lifecycle
is very archaic, very human-driven, very much,
call it a sequential process.
In the world of agentic, I mean, we
see two paths-- one is the technical path of it,
which, as you mentioned, Matt, there's memory,
the infrastructure.
Are we going to deploy it on our cloud, or public cloud,
or things like that?
So you have all these technical choices.
But a really key thing are the business choices.
Because what I tend to see, and again, this
is maybe another area of opportunity
for the entrepreneurial folks, today, there's
only a handful of companies that are
building frontier intelligence.
Literally, a handful of companies.
But there's going to be a slew of companies
that will be building, call it the engine
to make it work in enterprises.
Because enterprises have many things.
They need security.
They need governance.
They need compliance.
Plus, also, again, going back to the home mortgage,
I don't know why I'm caught up on the home mortgage example
today, but generally, the leaders would say,
OK, we have this large process.
Can you use AI and make it simpler, faster, better,
more automated?
And that is typically the wrong approach.
The approach would be, what is the art of possible using AI?
And can we reimagine this whole experience
and then again, find a way to go from your current process
to that?
And I see that as a gap in the enterprise.
Actually, Nikhil and I were talking in the green room.
When you talk to developers or product managers,
everyone individually claims that they are maybe 30% more
efficient right there, writing code faster than ever before.
But for some cases, you will not see
that translate into workflows.
So generally, it would or it should, but it doesn't always.
So I think that's where the gap is.
The gap is process engineering, understanding
the domain-specific data, understanding the use cases,
and then making sure you can work backwards into what would
be the right architecture.
Because the architecture, I think,
is going to start becoming the easier factor in all of this.
MATT CARBONARA: Yeah, it sounds like it's
as most problems, not just technology,
but people and process as well, which can be challenging.
I guess, the next question would be more around,
when you think about the organizational element
and having agents in the organization,
how do you see that?
And you touched on this, somewhat,
but curious what you both think about,
what does team composition look like?
How do you think about the ratio of employees
to agents to get a certain job done?
How does that impact how you think
about building your organizations
or evolving your organizations going forward?
I've seen some companies that have
adopted some agentic technologies
and not necessarily gotten the benefits versus companies that
have started with a clean sheet of paper
and adopted those technologies because of the legacy
that they have from an organizational perspective not
being able to take advantage of that.
So Nikhil, maybe you first, to hear how you guys at Circle
think about org design with agents as a new employee
or a new member of a team.
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: So we're just rolling out
the ability for employees to self-publish agents.
So we're in the process of rolling out an agent gateway,
so you know what all the agents are, and you can talk to them,
you can find them in Slack and connect with them.
Right now, I don't foresee a future
in which the point person on a project is not a human.
It is going to be a human.
A human can then go and invoke all from one
of the many agents we have inside this company,
query our agent gateway, figure out,
hey, what are all the agents available inside the company?
What finance agent do we have?
What marketing agent do we have?
And compose them into some kind of solution.
I don't think about it as an org design question,
because I don't tell the people working for me how many Google
Docs they can open or how many Google presentations they
can open.
They can do whatever they want.
They are creating an outcome for us.
So self-publish being able to access data,
so that you can self-publish, and being
able to have all the right ACLs, so you can self-publish,
and having all the agent communication figured out,
that is what I am focused on.
The org design is like, I don't care.
I really think, if you have an agent that can do something,
then I'm sure you can do something else for me.
MATT CARBONARA: Yeah.
Yeah.
I guess, it'll work itself out.
You'll just evolve based on--
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: Work itself out.
I do think organizations will be more productive, which is, I
think, everybody's experience.
Maybe they will reorganize because function A
versus function B is like now when the lines are blurrier.
And so I do think the organizational impact
for us is much more about like, well,
how do we compose our teams?
And like, who are the people?
Do the product managers do more product marketing?
Do product marketing do more brand?
Do BD do more product?
There's all kinds of questions like on sales calls,
like, who's showing up on sales calls?
You don't need a product person showing up.
Maybe our agent shows up on sales calls and gets notes.
So there's all kinds of efficiencies like this
that are being figured out.
But yeah, in terms of org design,
like old school McKinsey stuff, we're not thinking about it.
MATT CARBONARA: Makes sense.
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: You go do what you need to do.
MATT CARBONARA: Makes sense.
And Faraz, in your role and in your past, when
you think about adopting agents at scale, what do you think
are the biggest challenges in organizations
to adopting them at scale?
FARAZ SHAFIQ: I think, apart from the technological
challenges, I think there's a very interesting concept
that we're starting to look at, which
is the fact that there are not going to be
any individual contributors.
So I don't know how many people in the room are ICs for the ones
that are working, but typically, I mean,
out of our bank of 200,000 employees, largely,
they're individual contributors.
But what does that mean?
That means the ICs now will be manager of agents.
And so people that are individual contributors today,
they're typically not used to delegating work,
they're typically used to owning it end to end.
They're fully responsible.
But now, at this point, if you, let's just
say, get a body of work, and you may be using ChatGPT, or Claude,
or any of the model, then again, you still own the work,
but you're delegating it.
And that is going to be the dominant way of working moving
forwards.
And so one thing that we're doing right now
is emphasize how everyone is going to be a manager.
And just like you give feedback to humans,
you need to give feedback and have mechanisms to give feedback
to your agents, to have a way to grow your agents
and get more out of them.
And that's just very new, because it is something
that the playbooks really don't exist.
You're not used to a world of no ICs and all managers.
So I just thought that was a very interesting snippet
that, again, we're working with our HR team on,
on how do we roll that out.
MATT CARBONARA: Yeah, it's fascinating.
It's fascinating.
And maybe one more question for both of you,
then we'll go to a final question.
There's been all this discussion in the news last maybe three,
four weeks, around, intelligence is becoming democratized,
even the open source models are getting closer and closer
to frontier.
But you, as an org that's using this technology,
need to think about where is your moat over time?
How do you continue to own the things that differentiate you
from your competitors?
So maybe talk about how that impacts
how you think about building product at Circle, Nikhil,
and for you, Faraz, at Wells Fargo.
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: Yeah.
I mean, look, we're much smaller than Wells Fargo, I think.
MATT CARBONARA: But you have aspirations.
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: Yeah, we have--
I think there are two orders of magnitude, at least,
in the engineering organization, bigger than us.
Look, I think of this as, I mean, there's always a race on.
Like you're in a race with somebody.
And now, suddenly, you can wear a jet pack,
if you can master the jet pack.
And you can take a lead over the rest of the competition.
They'll catch up.
They will wear their jet pack.
And they will get there as well.
So first, I want to make sure that I put my jet
pack on before, and I get my organization
to put on the jet pack before everybody else does.
So we're very focused on that.
So how do we do that?
And second, you're right, a lot of stuff will get commoditized.
I think, software-only businesses,
I think this is broad consensus around this.
They will be hard to defend.
So we do have some hard things, though.
We are a company of networks.
USDC is our core product.
We think about it as a stablecoin network.
We have a payments network on top
of that, which is we call the Circle Payments Network.
And then we're building a new blockchain, which
is called Arc, which is also a network because you need
validators and you need participants
who are aligning incentives to participate in that blockchain.
So we believe these network businesses
are superior to software businesses.
And software is an enabler of these network businesses.
And how can we utilize the software
to build these software-enabled networks,
essentially, which then also have
a component that is really difficult.
For some of our blockchain stuff,
it's hard computational stuff.
For issuing a stablecoin, it's complicated.
You are chartered by the OCC.
And you have to submit to the exams.
So I almost think about it as the hard physics
of the business.
And then there's everything else.
And the hard physics of the business, we're
very focused on making sure that we do a really good job.
And getting into more businesses that are adjacencies,
that are also hard physics.
And then using this accelerant that we have on the top.
MATT CARBONARA: Awesome.
Makes sense.
FARAZ SHAFIQ: So I think there's going
to be some amazing changes that we will see, for sure,
in the banking industry.
And many of those things are not technological challenges,
by the way.
Like 24/7 trading, why does the trading end at 4:00 PM Eastern?
Why doesn't it continue going on?
And the answer, largely, is not technological,
it is not a big issue to technologically enable that.
It is that the regulators want to make sure
that the movement of money is regulated,
they're protecting the consumers,
and there's all these guardrails around that.
So you want to control those guardrails.
Just like self-driving is moving at an incredibly fast pace,
especially living here in the Bay Area,
we witnessed it probably more than others.
And same thing, why is money not,
let's just say, instantly available anywhere in the world,
at a click of a button?
So a lot of these, there's good technological solutions,
but it's more to, hey, yes, I can make the money available.
What if the other bank is taking two days to close the book?
Who's paying for that delta of two days?
And what happens when the money doesn't reach?
So it's all those other things.
So I think there's the regulatory part of it,
which has to catch up.
So we're going to see some new use cases as soon as we
see better regulation catch up.
And I think Nikhil said it really well that the software
side of it is going to make us do the hardware
side of the business really well.
And when I say hardware, I don't mean GPUs,
I know it's an agentic AI conference.
But we still have 4,000 branches.
We still believe that there's a value in human connection,
in having someone come in and talk to a bank advisor
in Spanish, because they only speak Spanish,
and build a plan for their financial education.
So we believe that those things are not going to go away.
It's just that how they are delivered and consumed
is going to dramatically change.
And over the course of time, I mean,
I honestly think that largely, we are dominated by LLMs today.
That's the talk of the town.
Eventually, it will be small language models,
it will be fine-tuned models, because that will become
as easy as a click of a button.
So today, it's all about token cost and LLMs.
Eventually, it'll be more about vertical specialized AI.
And so we're going to see a lot of new use cases come from that.
MATT CARBONARA: OK.
Awesome.
Final question, just to look ahead.
Looking ahead five years, what workflow in your domain
will be automatable that today, you
wouldn't imagine would be automatable for both of you?
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: You can go.
FARAZ SHAFIQ: [CHUCKLES] Oh, that's a tough one.
The amount of time today, we spend on, for example,
things like underwriting, because underwriting
is the core for any banks.
It doesn't matter if you're doing income verification, home
loan verification.
And it's a very archaic process.
People bring in all sorts of documentation.
You may send a utility bill that you
took a picture at a wrong angle, with the light hitting it,
and so someone has to send it back.
Very complex multimodal challenge.
I think that's just going to become table stakes with these
over the next couple of years.
And again, it's a compute challenge as well as
the economics are just not there.
So I think long-term, that'll be pretty big.
I do think eventually, by the way, today,
as I mentioned, LLMs are dominant eventually,
be small language models and fine-tune models.
And then quantum, once that compute is available,
we'll give an extra adrenaline to that.
MATT CARBONARA: Awesome.
Thank you.
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: Yeah.
I'm AGI build, so I believe we will be looking at AGI
through our bedroom windows.
And so at that point, who am I to say what is not solvable?
I will say one thing, it may be a data center full of geniuses,
but the humans are Byzantine.
They are idiosyncratic.
They are very hard to coordinate.
So it may be very lonely for those data centers
full of geniuses, while the rest of us
try to coordinate and figure this out.
So there is that.
We have really good models, but I
am surprised by how much effort it
takes just to convince people to do things,
even when those things are objectively good for them.
And so, I mean, I don't know if anybody
has a parent who you've tried to get them to eat their medicine.
It is objectively good for them to eat their medicine,
they will refuse.
Or children, for that matter.
Human society is not ready to just take it from these data
centers full of geniuses.
That is my conclusion.
I want those data centers around.
And I'm very glad that they are here,
but we have a lot of problems to solve
between now and this future that we're imagining.
MATT CARBONARA: Awesome.
Well, thank you, both.
Please help me thank Nikhil and Faraz.
NIKHIL CHANDHOK: Thank you.
FARAZ SHAFIQ: Thank you.
Thank you so much.
